terminal_record.title: State Department Title VIII Research Program Loses Federal Funding in 2013
terminal_record.description_short: The State Department’s Title VIII program for Eurasian and Eastern European language training and research lost its FY2013 appropriation.
terminal_record.description_medium: In 2013, the State Department’s Title VIII program for language training and research in Eurasian and Eastern European studies did not receive an appropriation for the federal fiscal year ending September 30. Contemporary reporting said the loss reduced fellowships and grants available in 2013–14. The evidence does not connect this Obama-era funding decision to Donald Trump.
terminal_record.description_long: In October 2013, Inside Higher Ed reported that Title VIII, a State Department program supporting language training and research in Eurasian and Eastern European studies, did not receive an appropriation for the federal fiscal year ending September 30. The Association for Slavic, East European and Eurasian Studies said the absence would reduce fellowships and grants available in 2013–14. The article reported that Title VIII funding averaged about $4.5 million annually in the early 2000s and had been cut to $3.3 million in fiscal year 2012. A 2014 PONARS Eurasia republication of Alexander Gabuev’s Guardian article says State Department leadership decided in fall 2013 not to allocate money for Russian studies after Congress changed the relevant budget wording from “shall” to “may.” Together, the reports support a narrow account of a 2013 funding decision. They do not support the original claim that cuts continued through 2015 to shift resources toward Syria, ISIS, and gun violence. The decision predates Donald Trump’s presidency, and the evidence reviewed establishes no connection to him. Whether this unrelated Obama-era event belongs in a Trump-focused collection remains an editorial scope question.

source_fact_map.source_excerpt: The Association for Slavic, East European and Eurasian Studies (ASEEES) has learned that the Title VIII program – a U.S. State Department program that funds language training and research in Eurasian and Eastern European studies – did not receive an appropriation for the federal fiscal year that ended Sept. 30. Because the money is typically allocated one year and spent the next, that means a significant reduction in the number of fellowships and grants available in 2013-14.
